stem:
With reference to hydroelectricity in North India, which of the following statements is/are correct ?
1. T here are huge possibilities of hydroelectricity in the Himalayan region.
2. Eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar cannot utilise this potential because the Himalayas situated to their North lies in boundary of Nepal.
Select the correct answer from the code given below :
Code :
expl: In the Himalayan region (Jammu & Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, etc.), rivers are fed by snow/glaciers as well as rainfall, so they are perennial. The steep gradient, narrow valleys, and landforms like waterfalls are suitable for large dams and run-of-the-river projects. Therefore, there is huge hydropower potential; hence statement 1 is correct. Most parts of eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar lie in the flat, low-gradient Gangetic plains. Even so, in eastern Uttar Pradesh, projects like Rihand exist in the Sonbhadra plateau/hilly region, and in Bihar, a run-of-the-river scheme like a Dagmara Hydroelectric Project on the Kosi is under progress. The fact that the Himalayas to the north lie in Nepal does not prevent utilization; through the national grid and inter-state/cross-border cooperation, such electricity can also be consumed by these states. Hence, statement 2 is false. According to UPPSC Correct answer is 'c'.

expl: The Himalayas are newly folded mountains of the Alpine orogeny, containing many of the world highest peaks. The height of the Himalayas is continuously increasing at a rate of approximately 5mm per year (according to some reliable soures, more than 1 cm per year). The Himalayas are young and tectonically active. Around 40-50 million years ago, when the Indian tectonic plate (a part of the larger Indo-Australian plate) moved northward (currently northeast) and collided with the Eurasian plate, the debris from the Tethys geosyncline between them was uplifted leading to the formation of the Himalayan mountain range.

expl: Major and vast rivers of the Indian subcontinent, such as the Indus, the Ganga and the Brahmaputra, originate from the Himalayan region (the main streams of the Ganga system emerge from Himalayan glaciers, while the Indus and the Brahmaputra originate north of the Himalayas—in the Trans-Himalayan/Tibetan region). These rivers maintain flow throughout the year; therefore, they are called perennial rivers. A major reason is that the highest Himalayan range—Greater Himalaya/Himadri—and the Trans-Himalayan ranges remain largely snow-covered throughout the year, and many glaciers originate from these ranges. Snow and glacier melt provide continuous water supply even in summer, while rainfall (especially monsoon rainfall) adds additional water. Thus, both (A) and (R) are correct, and (R) directly explains (A), because the presence of high, snow-covered ranges and associated glaciers plays a decisive role (as a major reason) in sustaining the perennial nature of Himalayan rivers.

stem: The Himalayas are formed of parallel fold ranges, of which the oldest range is –
expl: On the basis of folds and age of formation, the Himalayas are divided into three parallel structural areas - 1. Great Himalaya 2. The Middle Himalayas 3. Shiwalik According to the above options, the Great Himalaya is the oldest range of Himalayas (Oligocene Epoch-37-24 million years ago). After this, the Middle Himalayas (Miocene- 24-5 million years ago) and Shiwalik (Pliocene Epoch- 5-2 million years ago) is the newest range among them that was formed.

stem:
If there were no Himalayan ranges, what would have been the most likely geographical impact on India?
1. Much of the country would experience the cold waves from Siberia.
2. Indo-gangetic plain would be devoid of such extensive alluvial soils.
3. The pattern of monsoon would be different from what it is at present.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
expl: If the Himalayan mountain range didn't most of India would have experienced cold waves coming from Siberia, the Indo-Gangetic Plain would have been deprived of such elab-orative alluvial soil and the monsoon pattern would have been different from the present pattern. Significantly, the Himalays as influence the monsoon pattern as they effec-tively intercept the summer monsoons coming from the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea. It leads to precipitation in the snow of rain. Also, the Indus, Ganga's and their tributaries flowing form the Himalayan region create alluvial plains through erosion and deposition.

stem: The flat plains along the sub-Himalayan region in North India, are called –
expl: The flat plains along the sub-Himalayan region in North India, are called Bhabar. It is a narrow belt only 8 to 16 kms in width and lying parallel to the Shiwalik foothills at the break-up of the slope. This zone is studded with pebbles and it consists of porous beds which have been laid down by the numerous streams as they descend down the hills. The porosity is so high that all streams lose themselves in the Bhabar. South of the Bhabar is the Tarai belt, with an approximate width of 15-30 km where most of the streams and rivers re-emerge without having any properly demarcated channel, thereby, creating marshy and swampy conditions known as the Tarai. This has a luxurious growth of natural vegetation and houses a varied wildlife.

stem: The Shiwalik range is primarily composed of which type of material ?
expl: The Shiwalik Range is mainly composed of unconsolidated sediments. It is a group of loose sedimentary deposits, formed largely from river-borne pebbles and gravel, alluvium, sand, and clay.

stem: The Lesser Himalaya is located between-
expl: The Himalayan Range consists of parallel mountain ranges. It includes Great Himalayas, Middle Himalaya and the Shiwalik. The mountain range which runs parallel between the Shiwalik in the south and the Great Himalayas in the north is classified as the Middle Himalayas, sometimes also called Lesser Himalaya or Himachal or Lower Himalayas. It has an intricate system of ranges that have an average width of 50 km having elevation varying from 3,700 to 4,500 m above sea level. Pir Panjal, the Dhauladhar, the Mussoorie Range, the Nag Tibba and Mahabharat are some of the important ranges of the Middle Himalaya.

stem: Which one of the following is the youngest mountain chain ?
expl: The Shiwalik Himalaya formed in the last stage of formation of Himalaya, thus they are considered as the youngest mountain range. It comprises the outermost range of the Himalayas and is also known as outer Himalayas. Flat scrapes, anticlinal crests and synclinal valleys are the chief characteristics of this range. The Shiwaliks are formed of great thickness of Mio-Pleistocene sand, gravels and conglomerates which have been brought by the rivers flowing from the higher ranges of the Himalayas. These have been folded and faulted by the earth movements. Shiwaliks have a different names in different areas like Jammu Hills in Jammu. Dafla, Miri, Abor and Mishmi Hills in Arunachal Pradesh.

stem: Which one of the following groups is the correct sequence of mountain peaks from east to west?
expl: The correct sequence of mountain peaks from east to west is: Kanchenjunga, Everest, Annapurna, Dhaulagiri. Kanchenjunga is the third tallest mountain in the world. Three of the five summits of the Kanchenjunga (main, central, and south) are situated on the boundary of the North Sikkim district in Sikkim, India and the Taplejung District in Nepal. The two other peaks are entirely situated in Taplejung District. Mt. Everest is the tallest mountain in the world above sea level. The elevation of Mount Everest is 8,848 meters (now 8848.86 m). The peak is situated in the Himalayas on the border of Nepal and China, which is also known as the Sagarmatha. The Annapurna region is an area in northcentral Nepal where some of the most popular treks are located. Dhaulagiri Peak is also located in West Central Nepal, west of Annapurna Peak.

expl: The Himalayas are spread over most of the northern and northeastern states & UTs i.e., Jammu & Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram and Tripura. stem:
Given below are two statements, one is labelled as
Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).
Assertion (A) : The highest concentration of Seismic zones lies in Himalayan region in India.
Reason (R) : There are many longitudinal thrust zones in Himalayas.
Codes :

options.label: a
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

options.label: b
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)

expl: The highest concentration of seismic zones in India lies in the Himalayan region. Most of the area lies in seismic zones IV and V. Under this region, the area of Northeast India, Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand is included. So we can say that the highest concentration of seismic zones lies in the Himalayan region in India. Hence, statement (a) is correct. Many longitudinal thrusts and faults lie in the Himalayas. The Main Frontal Thrust (MFT) lies when moving from south to north. Between MFT and MBF (Main Boundary Fault), there is an extension of Sub-Himalayan (Shiwalik). Between MBF and MCT (Main Central Thrust) there is an extension of the Lesser Himalayas. Above this is the extension of Greater Himalayas, which is also known as the CCZ (Central Crystalline Zone). HHC (Higher Himalayan Crystalline) is located above the MCT Tibet Himalaya is situated between HHC and STDS (South Tibetan Detachment System). The Himalaya lies to the north of ITSA Due to the location of the reverse region and the Himalayan geographical structure, it becomes the most concentrated earthquake zone in India. Due to the operation of plates in this area, it is an earthquake-prone area.
